scenes.headline: Data Types & Collections
scenes.subtitle: The containers that hold your data
scenes.narration: Python offers several built-in types for storing and organizing data, and choosing the right one matters for both correctness and speed.

scenes.headline: Everyday scalar types
scenes.narration: Integers and floats cover whole numbers and decimals, and mixing them up can cause rounding surprises in calculations. The str type holds text of any length, from a single character to a whole document. A bool is either True or False and drives every conditional decision your code makes. And None is Python's way of representing the deliberate absence of a value, which is distinct from zero or an empty string.

scenes.headline: Choosing a collection
scenes.narration: A list keeps an ordered sequence you reach into by position, which is ideal when order matters or you need to iterate in sequence. A dictionary instead maps keys to values, giving you near-instant lookups when you know the key you want. In practice you reach for a list when the data is a sequence of records and a dict when you need to look things up by name or id.

scenes.headline: Working with collections
scenes.narration: We start with a list of servers and use append to add a new one to the end, since lists are mutable. Then we build a config dictionary that pairs each setting name with its value. Reading the port back out is just a key lookup, and these two operations power most everyday data scripts.

scenes.headline: Mutable versus immutable
scenes.narration: Some collections such as lists, dictionaries and sets are mutable, meaning you can change their contents in place after they are created. Others like strings and tuples are immutable, so any change actually produces a brand-new object. Reaching for an immutable type is a good choice when you want data to stay constant and safe from accidental edits.

scenes.headline: When to use a set
scenes.narration: A set stores only unique items, so adding a value that already exists simply does nothing. Because of how it is built, checking whether something is in a set is almost instant even for large collections. The trade-off is that a set has no order, so you cannot index into it the way you can a list. That makes sets perfect for de-duplication and for tracking which ids you have already seen.

scenes.text: Match the collection to your access pattern: lists for order, dicts for lookups, sets for uniqueness.
scenes.narration: The takeaway is to match the collection to how you will actually use the data, choosing lists for order, dicts for lookups and sets for uniqueness.
